newsitem.title: UK: Brady market frowns at Bulgaria, smiles on Russia.
newsitem.headline: Brady market frowns at Bulgaria, smiles on Russia.

text.p: Bulgaria got a fresh battering on the emerging debt market on Thursday but, for a brief moment, Russia paper surged to a new high in a market which is generally firm but on tenterhooks as it awaits U.S. payrolls figures.
Bulgaria has plunged this week on growing fears that its economy be heading for disaster after the International Monetary Fund delayed payment of the August tranche of a loan.
"The whole country story is extremely weak and worrying. Just because it is cheap doesn't mean it can't get cheaper," West Merchant Bank economic adviser Peter West said.
Bulgarian IABs BGFLTH11=RR, bid 1/8 of a point lower on Thursday, have slumped more than 11 percent since the middle of August and over 20 percent since the start of the year.
Analysts have increasingly warned of the dangers that Bulgaria could default next year when it has some $1.4 billion in foreign debt service payments.
But some say the chances of the IMF pulling the rug from under Bulgaria are very remote and that the debt's enormous yield compared to the rest of the market keeps it an attractive buy.
"I like it. It will not default...it's not a positive credit story but if you don't think it will default why not hold it," said Bank of America senior trader Michael Jordan.
He pointed to current yields on the debt of up to 15 percent while spreads for IABs over U.S. Treasuries are around 1,500 basis points.
By delaying payment, the IMF was ensuring that when it did provide the money Bulgaria would use it to service its Bradys and not for some other purpose, he added.
"We think that the government will again give in to the IMF and finally receive the next loan," CS Frist Boston said in its weekly update.
"But this would not offer a solution in the long term as an increase in the VAT would fuel further the existing inflationary spiral," it said.
Russian debt briefly hit a new high in early trading with Vneshekonombank dollar paper RUVNUSLNS=RR trading at 63-1/4 cents in the dollar.
But it quickly dropped back to around 62-1/2 cents.
Traders noted rumours that a U.S. fund had decided to increase its Russia allocation and there was no particular fresh news out of Russia to lend support.

However, creditor approval to turn the Vnesh old Soviet debt into loans is all but certain and as the risk diminishes that the deal will not go through, so the price has risen along with interest in the principal loan and interest arrears notes that the debt will turn into probably towards the end of this year.
One creditor source, involved in the rescheduling negotiations, said the process of settling the debt appeared to be going ahead without any hitches though at a rather slow pace.
A key attraction for investors at the moment is Russia's impending Eurobond issue, planned for November, which should help to bring up Vnesh prices.

The rest of the market is firm, though few traders are prepared to do much ahead of Friday's U.S. non-farm payrolls data which is expected to be the sign for whether U.S. interest rates are headed for a rise.
The West Merchant Bank index for the Brady market is almost back to its end-August peak and, at 156.28, very close to the all-time high of 160.89 reached on January 13, 1994.
-- Jonathan Thatcher, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7770 (fax +44 171 583 7239)
